question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and tenderness. The pain began approximately 2 days ago in the area just above his umbilicus and was crampy in nature. Earlier this morning, the pain moved laterally to his right lower abdomen. At that time, the pain in the right lower quadrant became severe and constant and woke him up from sleep. He decided to come to the hospital. The patient is nauseous and had a low-grade fever of 37.8°C (100.1°F). Other vitals are normal. Upon physical examination, the patient has rebound tenderness but a negative psoas sign while the remaining areas of his abdomen are non-tender. His rectal exam is normal. Laboratory tests show a white cell count of 15,000/mm3. Urinalysis and other laboratory findings were negative. What conclusion can be drawn about the nerves involved in the transmission of this patient’s pain during the physical exam?

options.opa: His pain is mainly transmitted by the right splanchnic nerve.
options.opb: His pain is transmitted bilaterally by somatic afferent nerve fibers of the abdomen.
options.opc: His pain is transmitted by somatic afferent nerve fibers located in the right flank.
options.opd: His pain is transmitted by right somatic nerve fibers.
options.ope: His pain is transmitted by the pelvic nerves.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: His pain began above umbilicus -> Moved to right lower abdomen -> Severe constant pain in right lower quadrant -> Rebound tenderness present -> Negative psoas sign -> Non-tender in other abdominal areas -> Normal rectal exam -> White cell count elevated -> 90% CHAIN: Pain progression suggests appendicitis -> Rebound tenderness and migration of pain typical -> Negative psoas sign common in appendicitis -> Non-tender in other areas -> Elevated white cell count indicative of inflammation -> 90%
enhanced_information: The patient's pain progression, rebound tenderness, migration of pain to the right lower quadrant, and elevated white cell count are consistent with appendicitis. The nerves involved in the transmission of his pain during the physical exam are likely somatic afferent nerve fibers associated with appendicitis, supporting option opc.
analysis: The patient's presentation with right lower quadrant pain, migration of pain, rebound tenderness, and elevated white cell count is highly suggestive of appendicitis. In appendicitis, the pain is typically transmitted by somatic afferent nerve fibers associated with the inflamed appendix, which are located in the right lower quadrant. The negative psoas sign and absence of tenderness in other areas of the abdomen further support this localization of pain. Therefore, the most likely correct option is opc.
